description: Master the repeatable 14-step battle-tested interview roadmap from requirement gathering to clean C++ code.

topics.title: The 14-Step Systematic Interview Roadmap
topics.definition: A battle-tested, structured 45-minute execution blueprint designed to navigate any ambiguous Low-Level Design interview smoothly from problem definition to working modern C++ code.
topics.why_it_matters: 80% of candidates fail LLD interviews not due to bad code, but due to jumping straight to coding before clarifying scope, missing edge cases, and producing rigid, untestable designs.
topics.real_world_analogy: An architectural construction process: no builder pours concrete without blueprints, client approval, load-bearing calculations, and plumbing schematics.
conceptual_breakdown: Phase 1: Clarification & Scope (0-8 min): Steps 1-4: Functional, Non-Functional, Use Cases, Scale.
Phase 2: Domain Modeling & OOP Design (8-20 min): Steps 5-8: Core Entities, Relationships, UML Class & Sequence Diagrams.
Phase 3: Design Patterns & Architecture (20-28 min): Step 9: Pattern Selection (Strategy, Observer, State, Factory).
Phase 4: Idiomatic C++ Coding (28-40 min): Steps 10-12: Header definitions, Thread Safety, Error Handling.
Phase 5: Defense & Verification (40-45 min): Steps 13-14: Concurrency edge cases, Extensibility walkthrough.

steps.description: Step 1-4: Gather requirements. Clarify constraints (e.g. multi-threading, scale, out of scope).
Step 5-8: Identify Entities. Draw UML Class Diagram with clear Association vs Composition.
Step 9: Choose Design Patterns (e.g. Strategy for algorithms, State for lifecycles).
Step 10-12: Write production-grade C++20 code with smart pointers and RAII.
Step 13-14: Walk through concurrency, exception safety, and unit testing.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Explicit Time Management: Dedicate no more than 8 minutes to scoping so at least 15 minutes remain for live coding.
2. Top-Down Verbal Alignment: Always validate entity choices and diagram relationships with the interviewer before writing code.
3. Modern C++ Best Practices: Demonstrate ownership semantics (`std::unique_ptr`, `std::shared_ptr`), RAII, and `std::mutex` discipline.

comparison_matrix.title: Interview Approaches
rows: Starts coding immediately, misses key limits
Tightly coupled classes with hardcoded switches
Forgotten or added as crude global lock
Clean per-entity or lock-free concurrency design

common_mistakes.mistake: Silently thinking and coding for 20 minutes without speaking
common_mistakes.correction: Think out loud continuously. Treat the interview as a collaborative design review with a senior colleague.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'The candidate finishes coding in 15 minutes with a monolithic 300-line main() function.'
Answer: Instant rejection. LLD interviews evaluate modularity, encapsulation, interface segregation, and design patterns, not fast scripting.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Identify the missing steps in an interview submission that jumps directly from problem prompt to raw C++ structs.
code_refactor_exercise.bad_code: struct ParkingLot { int spots[100]; }; // No interface, no strategies, no tests
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: Establish IParkingStrategy, Vehicle hierarchies, and thread synchronization.

practice_problem.title: Timeboxed 30-Minute Mock Interview
practice_problem.description: Apply the 14-step framework to design an In-Memory File System within a strict 30-minute timer.
practice_problem.hint: Spend: 5m Clarify, 8m UML, 12m Code, 5m Concurrency & Verification.

topics.title: Step 1-4: Clarification & Domain Decomposition
topics.definition: Techniques for asking probing questions to define precise system boundaries, distinguish functional from non-functional requirements, and establish entity vocabularies.
topics.why_it_matters: Real-world engineering problems are inherently ambiguous. Demonstrating that you know which clarifying questions to ask proves senior-level engineering maturity.
topics.real_world_analogy: A doctor conducting patient intake: before prescribing surgery, they gather medical history, check allergies, and evaluate vital signs.
conceptual_breakdown: Functional Requirements (FR): What the system MUST do (e.g. Park vehicle, dispense ticket, calculate fee).
Non-Functional Requirements (NFR): Performance, Concurrency, Latency, Extensibility, Thread-safety.
Out of Scope: Explicitly agreeing on features NOT to build (e.g. Physical hardware drivers, web UI, database migrations).
Scale & Constraints: Single machine in-memory vs distributed, QPS, memory footprint.

steps.description: Candidate asks: 'Should we support multiple entrance gates operating simultaneously?'
Interviewer confirms: 'Yes, assume 4 gates concurrently parking cars.'
Candidate notes: 'Adding thread-safety (NFR) via fine-grained spot mutexes.'

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Define What is IN and OUT of Scope: Prevents scope creep and ensures alignment within the first 5 minutes.
2. Identify Core Actions & Actors: Formulate use cases as: Actor -> Action -> System Result.
3. Establish Strong Domain Types: Use custom structs instead of raw `int` or `string` for IDs.

comparison_matrix.title: Requirement Scoping Techniques
rows: 'Will multiple entrance gates park vehicles concurrently, and what is the expected write contention rate?'
'Should pricing be extensible to support dynamic peak-hour surges or EV kilowatt-hour billing via a Strategy pattern?'
'Should we design this as a pure in-memory domain model with repository interfaces for future persistence?'

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming single-threaded execution without asking the interviewer

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Candidate asks 25 questions and uses up 18 minutes of a 45-minute interview.'
Answer: Limit initial clarification to 4-5 high-impact questions; state reasonable assumptions for the rest and confirm them.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Convert ambiguous primitive arguments into explicit domain value objects.
code_refactor_exercise.bad_code: void book(int a, string b, double c);
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: void book(SeatId seat, UserId user, Price amount);

practice_problem.title: Formulate 5 Core Clarifying Questions for a Hotel Booking System
practice_problem.description: Write down the 5 essential functional and non-functional questions you would ask before designing a Hotel Reservation engine.
practice_problem.hint: Cover room types, multi-room party reservations, cancellation policies, overbooking tolerance, and concurrent booking locks.

topics.title: Step 5-9: Drawing Class & Sequence Diagrams Live
topics.definition: Visualizing domain models rapidly using standard UML class notations (attributes, methods, visibility), relationships (Inheritance, Composition, Aggregation, Association), and interaction sequence diagrams.
topics.why_it_matters: A clear UML diagram allows the interviewer to spot architectural flaws in 30 seconds before a single line of C++ code is written, saving 20 minutes of costly code refactoring.
topics.real_world_analogy: An electrical schematic: symbols clearly indicate resistors, capacitors, and power lines before fabricating the physical circuit board.
conceptual_breakdown: UML Class Notation: Class name, attributes with visibility (`-` private, `+` public, `#` protected), methods.
Relationship Symbols: Composition (filled diamond - lifetime bound), Aggregation (hollow diamond - shared pointer), Inheritance (hollow triangle).
Sequence Diagrams: Lifeline columns, synchronous calls, asynchronous events, return arrows.
Design Pattern Integration: Annotating interfaces with `<>` and strategy links.

steps.description: Candidate identifies entities: Room, Booking, Guest, PricingStrategy.
Draws Composition: Booking OWNS Guest details. Hotel OWNS Rooms.
Draws Strategy Interface for dynamic pricing.
Interviewer reviews and approves architecture. Candidate transitions to coding.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Translating Composition to C++: Use std::unique_ptr or direct value member variables for strong lifecycle ownership.
2. Translating Aggregation to C++: Use std::shared_ptr or std::weak_ptr for shared or non-owning references.
3. Abstract Interfaces: Use pure virtual classes with virtual ~Class() = default;.

comparison_matrix.title: Diagramming Fidelity in Interviews
rows: Easy to review on web whiteboard
High chance of major mid-interview rewrites

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing Association, Aggregation, and Composition in UML
common_mistakes.correction: Composition = exclusive ownership (delete parent destroys child); Aggregation = shared reference (child can exist independently).

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Why did you choose an inheritance hierarchy for SpotType instead of an enum attribute?'
Answer: Explain polymorphism trade-offs: if spots have unique behavior (e.g. EV spots need metering telemetry), use inheritance; if they only differ by dimensions, an enum attribute is simpler and cleaner.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Convert a messy circular pointer dependency in UML into a clean mediator or observer design.
code_refactor_exercise.bad_code: Class A owns B, Class B owns A (shared_ptr cycle)
code_refactor_exercise.good_code: Class B holds weak_ptr to A or uses Observer callback.

practice_problem.title: Draw UML Diagram for an Amazon Locker System
practice_problem.description: Design the class diagram for Amazon Locker: LockerSize, LockerSlot, Package, DeliveryCode, and LockerHub.
practice_problem.hint: LockerHub has Composition of LockerSlots; LockerSlot has Aggregation (0..1) of Package.

topics.title: Step 10-14: Live C++ Coding & Concurrency Defense
topics.definition: Executing the live coding phase cleanly using modern C++20 idioms: RAII, smart pointer ownership, const-correctness, thread safety guarantees, and defending design choices against edge cases.
topics.why_it_matters: The final test of execution. Writing clean, compiling, idiomatic C++ with zero memory leaks and proper lock scopes differentiates top-tier candidates from average ones.
topics.real_world_analogy: A master craftsman assembling precision watch gears: every piece fits snugly, springs have exact tension, and lubrication ensures frictionless movement under high load.
conceptual_breakdown: Exception Safety: Strong vs Basic guarantee; avoid throwing in destructors.
Extensibility Defense: Walk the interviewer through how a new feature can be added with ZERO modifications to existing classes (OCP).

steps.description: Candidate writes clean header declarations with nodiscard and smart pointers.
Applies std::lock_guard to critical sections protecting state invariants.
Interviewer asks: 'How do you add PayPal support tomorrow?' Candidate explains OCP via IPaymentProcessor.
Interviewer asks: 'What happens during sudden thread cancellation?' Candidate highlights RAII lock unwinding.

step_by_step_explanation: 1. Modern Rule of 5 Discipline: Explicitly deleting copy constructors prevents accidental mutex copy or object slicing.
2. Reader-Writer Lock Optimization: std::shared_lock allows 1,000 threads to read concurrently without contention.
3. Value Semantics and Move Semantics: Passing by value and moving with std::move() achieves optimal performance for both rvalues and lvalues.
4. Clean Optional Return Types: std::optional clearly communicates potential absence of data without using magic null pointers.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing `new` without a matching `delete` in interview whiteboard code
common_mistakes.correction: Never use raw `new` in modern C++. Use `std::make_unique` or `std::make_shared`.

common_mistakes.mistake: Unlocking mutex manually at end of function instead of using RAII lock guards
common_mistakes.correction: If an exception throws or early return triggers, manual unlock is skipped causing permanent deadlock.

interview_traps:
Trap: 'Why did you use std::lock_guard instead of std::unique_lock?'
Answer: `std::lock_guard` is lighter with zero runtime overhead when you don't need manual unlocking, deferring, or condition variables; use `std::unique_lock` when pairing with `std::condition_variable`.

code_refactor_exercise.problem: Refactor legacy C++ code with raw pointers and manual mutex locks into modern idiomatic C++20.
code_refactor_exercise.bad_code: Resource* r = new Resource(); mtx.lock(); list.push_back(r); mtx.unlock();

practice_problem.title: Implement Thread-Safe Bounded Stack
practice_problem.description: Write a complete `ThreadSafeBoundedStack<T, Capacity>` using `std::mutex`, `std::condition_variable`, and `std::optional<T>`.
practice_problem.hint: Block `push` when full; block `pop` when empty.
